chapters.title: Snapshot
chapters.body:
# Snapshot

## What the company is

Sivers Semiconductors AB (ticker: SIVE.ST; OTC US: SIVEF) is a Swedish holding company with two operating subsidiaries that share almost nothing except a parent. **Sivers Wireless AB** makes millimeter-wave beamformers and antenna modules for SATCOM, 5G/6G, and defense applications, claiming to be the only EU-based commercial provider in several beamformer categories; named customers include the European Space Agency and Intelsat. **Sivers Photonics Ltd.** — the UK subsidiary acquired in 2017 as CST Global — designs custom high-power indium-phosphide distributed-feedback lasers and laser arrays, and it is increasingly positioned as the upstream chokepoint for the External Light Source modules that enable co-packaged optics in next-generation AI data-center GPUs. The two businesses share a balance sheet, a Nasdaq Stockholm listing, and an ambition to dual-list in New York. Everything else — technology, geography, customer base — diverges.

At SEK 72.90 × 311.33 million shares outstanding, the market capitalisation sits at approximately SEK 22.7 billion, or roughly $2.2 billion at current exchange rates. That figure warrants an immediate caveat: analyst writeups circulating in early 2025 cited a market cap of around SEK 3.4 billion — a number that, at the time, may have been accurate but has since been rendered obsolete by a rally that accelerated through the CPO narrative. Readers relying on older secondary sources should reset their mental model accordingly.

## Seventy-five years, three acts

Founded in 1951 by engineer Carl von Sivers as Sivers Lab AB, manufacturing passive microwave products. Philips Sweden acquired it in 1960, merged it in 1983 with IMA AB to create Sivers IMA, and a management buyout extracted it from Philips in 1990. Two acquisitions created the modern entity: CST Global in 2017 (the Scottish III-V photonics specialist that became Sivers Photonics) and MixComm in 2022 (a US-based millimeter-wave startup). Chapter 2 details the full history.

## The management team that matters for the US listing

Vickram Vathulya — PhD from Lehigh, MBA from Berkeley Haas, 25 years across NXP, Maxim, and Nuvotronics — was appointed President and CEO on August 19, 2024, with a personal commitment to purchase up to $1 million in stock. Executive Chairman Bami Bastani, a 42-year semiconductor veteran and three-time public-company turnaround CEO, joined as Strategic Advisor in August 2023 and moved to Executive Chairman in February 2024. Chapter 6 maps the full leadership team and the board reshuffle underway.

## FY2025: growth, but deeper losses after accounting restatement

The full-year 2025 results, published May 13, 2026, had been restated under PCAOB-aligned standards as preparation for the potential US dual listing.

| Metric | Swedish K3 (original) | PCAOB-restated |
|---|---|---|
| Net sales (SEK M) | 304.1 | 306.6 |
| EBIT (SEK M) | −141.3 | −177.8 |
| Net loss (SEK M) | −186.5 | −222.6 |
| EPS (SEK) | −0.69 | −0.81 |
| Equity per share (SEK) | 3.46 | 3.05 |

Revenue grew 25% year-on-year (33% constant currency) to SEK 306.6 million. The sales pipeline expanded 64% to $453 million. Free cash outflow narrowed to SEK 66 million from SEK 151 million in 2022. Cash at year-end was SEK 43.5 million — thin — subsequently topped up by a $17 million refinancing with [Bootstrap Europe](https://news.cision.com/sivers-semiconductors/r/sivers-semiconductors-refinances-group-debt-facilities-with-bootstrap-europe-to-strengthen-capital-s,c4312725) and a non-dilutive $6.6 million NEMC Year 2 grant. Chapter 4 dissects the restatement mechanics; Chapter 5 traces the five quarters that built the rally.

## The question the rest of this report answers

Is Sivers the next LITE — the chokepoint pattern repeating, where a small western laser maker becomes structurally indispensable as hyperscalers standardize on co-packaged optics — or is the at-the-peak valuation pricing a CPO volume ramp that has not yet shipped a single production module? The June 15, 2026 AGM, where shareholders vote on a 15% dilution authority and a board reshuffle that clears out co-founder Fällström, is the first concrete test of whether management can deliver on the architecture they have been promising since 2024.

chapters.title: From Sivers Lab to Sivers Photonics — 75 years
chapters.body:
# From Sivers Lab to Sivers Photonics — 75 years

## A passive-microwave shop in Stockholm, 1951

Carl von Sivers founded Sivers Lab AB in Sweden in 1951 to make passive microwave components — slotted-line VSWR detectors and the instrumentation that surrounds them. It was artisanal, specialized work, serving defence laboratories and university physics departments across Scandinavia. Nine years later, in 1960, Philips Sweden absorbed the company, and Sivers Lab effectively disappeared into a multinational for what would prove to be a long, under-documented interval.

The thread re-emerges in 1983, when Philips merged Sivers Lab with IMA AB — a Stockholm-based maker of microwave components and oscillators for radar applications, founded in 1975 — to create Sivers IMA, a producer of magnetically tunable filters and oscillators using yttrium-iron-garnet (YIG) technology. Seven years later, in 1990, the management bought the company out of Philips through a vehicle called SI Holding AB, restoring it as an independent supplier ([Sivers history page](https://www.sivers-semiconductors.com/company-2/history/)). The 1990s saw a divestment of high-power microwave operations and the acquisition of the Swedish filter maker Lyscom; the 2000s and early 2010s brought low-phase-noise products, ultra-wideband VCOs, and the proprietary millimetre-wave converters that would eventually anchor the wireless subsidiary. Sivers IMA Holding AB began trading on Nasdaq First North Stockholm on 30 November 2017, moving to the main Nasdaq Stockholm board on 10 June 2021.

## The foundational move: CST Global, 2017

Everything that makes Sivers interesting to investors today traces back to a single acquisition. In 2017, Sivers IMA Holding bought [CST Global](https://www.sivers-semiconductors.com/), a Scottish manufacturer of III-V photonic devices with its own R&D facility and clean-room fabrication capacity outside Glasgow. CST Global supplied photonic components in wafer, coated bar, chip device, and die-on-tape formats — bespoke, low-volume, high-specification work for customers who could not or would not go to the large Asian foundries.

The renamed subsidiary, Sivers Photonics Ltd., gave the group something no amount of microwave-component iteration could have produced: a captive, western-domiciled source of indium phosphide distributed-feedback (InP DFB) lasers. DFB lasers at specific C-band wavelengths (1530–1565 nm) are the light engines inside the transceiver modules that carry data through fibre. In 2017, that was a niche. By 2025 it was a chokepoint.

Two years after the CST deal closed, Sivers Photonics and imec announced a collaboration to integrate C-band InP DFB laser arrays directly onto imec's silicon photonics platform. The work pointed squarely toward the co-packaged optics architecture that hyperscalers would not start seriously deploying for another five years.

## Wireless expansion and the rebrand

In 2022, the group acquired MixComm, a US-based millimetre-wave startup, bolting it into the Sivers Wireless AB subsidiary alongside the legacy beamformer and phased-array business. MixComm brought additional customers in 5G fixed wireless, SATCOM, and defence. Two years earlier, in 2020, the parent had renamed itself Sivers Semiconductors AB and consolidated the operating entities under their current names — Sivers Wireless AB (mmWave RF) and Sivers Photonics Ltd. (DFB lasers).

## The American turn

The signals pointing toward a US capital-markets strategy began appearing in mid-2023. In August of that year, Bami Bastani joined the board as a Strategic Advisor. By February 2024 he was Executive Chairman of Sivers Inc. and Chairman of Sivers AB. Six months later, in August 2024, Vickram Vathulya replaced Anders Storm as CEO. (Chapter 6 carries the leadership detail in full.)

## 2025–26: the accounting signal

On 13 May 2026, the group published its [2025 Annual Report with PCAOB-restated financials](https://www.sivers-semiconductors.com/press/sivers-semiconductors-publishes-the-2025-annual-report-adjusting-prior-reported-financials-as-preparation-for-a-potential-dual-listing-in-the-united-states/), explicitly framed as preparation for a potential Nasdaq New York dual listing. The mechanics of the restatement are dissected in Chapter 4.

A $6.6 million NEMC Year 2 grant from the US Department of Defense, announced on 19 May 2026, reinforced the American vector. An AGM scheduled for June 2026 carries a 15% dilution authority vote and a board reshuffle suggesting the capital structure is still being shaped for whatever the dual-listing roadshow requires.

---

Sivers spent roughly 65 years as a passive-microwave shop before two acquisitions in five years turned it into what its current management is betting will prove to be a laser chokepoint in the AI optical-interconnect supply chain. The pace of transformation is the story.

chapters.title: Two subsidiaries, two supply chains
chapters.body:
# Two subsidiaries, two supply chains

## One competency, two markets

The two wholly-owned subsidiaries — Sivers Wireless AB in Stockholm and Sivers Photonics Ltd. in Glasgow — serve structurally different end-markets yet share a single underlying materials competency: the fabrication of compound III-V semiconductors, primarily indium phosphide (InP) and gallium arsenide (GaAs), into precision radio-frequency and photonic components. That shared substrate is the reason the company exists as a unified entity rather than two separate listings.

The two segments look almost nothing alike commercially. Wireless sells into long-cycle institutional procurement — space agencies, satellite operators, defense primes — where design wins are slow and revenue is lumpy but durable. Photonics sells into a hypergrowth AI-infrastructure cycle where the purchase decision moves at datacenter speed and the volumes, if they materialise, dwarf anything the wireless book has ever seen.

## Sivers Wireless AB: the institutional floor

The wireless subsidiary produces millimetre-wave (mmWave) beamformers, phased-array integrated circuits, and antenna modules for four principal applications: satellite communications (SATCOM), fixed wireless access (FWA), 5G/6G base station infrastructure, and defence and aerospace.

The strongest claim management makes about this segment is that Sivers Wireless is the only EU-based commercial provider of certain beamformer types — specifically those meeting the performance and supply-chain sovereignty requirements of European institutional SATCOM buyers. That claim is difficult to verify independently but is consistent with the named customer roster: the [European Space Agency](https://www.sivers-semiconductors.com/) and Intelsat. Both represent buyers for whom a European-domiciled supplier with traceable fabrication is a procurement requirement. The $6.6 million Year 2 NEMC grant establishes Sivers Wireless inside the US Department of Defense supplier ecosystem — a prerequisite for any future prime-contractor relationship.

The wireless segment is not, on its own, a growth story. Its value to the consolidated entity is stability and credibility: recurring institutional customers, a defensible geographic chokepoint in European SATCOM procurement, and a foothold in US defence that provides non-dilutive grant revenue while the photonics business scales.

## Sivers Photonics Ltd.: the CPO thesis

Sivers Photonics makes high-power indium phosphide DFB (distributed feedback) lasers, laser arrays, optical amplifiers, and increasingly the External Light Source (ELS) modules that bundle those lasers into a form factor that can be integrated directly into an optical interposer or co-packaged optics assembly.

For CPO applications, lasers must satisfy three simultaneous constraints: continuous-wave (CW) rather than pulsed; monochromatic and wavelength-stable (DFB gratings lock emission to within a fraction of a nanometre); and high-power, because the optical signal will be split across multiple channels before reaching its destination.

The substrate of choice for these lasers at telecom-band wavelengths — 1.31 microns and 1.55 microns — is indium phosphide. Silicon photonics cannot efficiently emit light at these wavelengths. Every silicon photonic chip still needs an external InP laser. Sivers Photonics is one of a small number of independent western foundries capable of custom-designing and small-batch manufacturing these components, which is what positions it as a chokepoint supplier rather than a commodity one.

## The LiDAR wildcard

The company has disclosed a strategic automotive FMCW LiDAR customer incorporating Sivers photonics technology "across all their platforms," with a production ramp targeted for Q4 2026 and lifecycle revenue estimated at $53–138 million over 8–10 years. The customer has not been named publicly. The unusually wide range suggests either significant uncertainty in volume forecasting or deliberate obfuscation to protect a sensitive commercial relationship. Q4 2026 production is the first concrete checkpoint.

## The financial picture — and its gaps

Sivers does not publish a clean segment revenue split. FY2025 product revenue of SEK 85.7 million grew only 13 percent at constant FX against the 33 percent growth of consolidated net sales. The gap implies that a significant portion of revenues derives from service contracts, licensing arrangements, and funded development agreements rather than shipped components — making the segment-level revenue story opaque.

## The segment-level verdict

Sivers Wireless is the historical floor and the institutional credibility anchor — European sovereign-supply position, named space-sector customers, and an emerging US defence pipeline. Sivers Photonics is the option value: direct design-win relationships across the emergent CPO supply chain, an automotive LiDAR wildcard, and a $453 million pipeline (64% YoY growth). Wireless funds the building; photonics is the reason anyone is in the room.

chapters.title: Two sets of books — and what the restatement actually means
chapters.body:
# Two sets of books — and what the restatement actually means

## The restatement in plain language

On 13 May 2026, Sivers Semiconductors published its 2025 Annual Report — nearly three months after preliminary results had already circulated. The delay was not accidental. Embedded in the document was a disclosure that should arrest any investor treating the prior numbers as a baseline: a full PCAOB-aligned restatement of both FY2025 and FY2024, prepared as groundwork for a potential US dual listing. The effect was material. The EBIT loss for FY2025 widened by SEK 36.5 million. The net loss deepened by SEK 36.1 million. Book equity fell by SEK 127 million. And the FY2024 figures — already unattractive — were revised to look considerably worse.

Two sets of books now exist. Neither is wrong in a legal sense: Swedish K3 accounting, which Sivers has always reported under, permits practices that PCAOB does not. But for investors evaluating the company on a pre-listing basis, the PCAOB-restated figures are the ones that matter for comparability with US-listed peers. They are also the more conservative set.

| Metric | As Reported (K3) | PCAOB-Restated | Δ |
|---|---|---|---|
| Net Sales (SEK M) | 304.1 | 306.6 | +2.5 |
| EBIT (SEK M) | −141.3 | −177.8 | −36.5 |
| Net Result (SEK M) | −186.5 | −222.6 | −36.1 |
| EPS (SEK) | −0.69 | −0.81 | −0.12 |
| Equity (SEK M) | 1,076.8 | 949.8 | −127.0 |
| Equity/Share (SEK) | 3.46 | 3.05 | −0.41 |

*FY2025 — [Sivers 2025 Annual Report](https://www.sivers-semiconductors.com/press/sivers-semiconductors-publishes-the-2025-annual-report-adjusting-prior-reported-financials-as-preparation-for-a-potential-dual-listing-in-the-united-states/)*

Revenue, curiously, moved slightly upward under PCAOB (SEK 304.1M → SEK 306.6M). That is not a comfort. It reflects the timing mechanics of the restatement: revenue was reallocated *out of* 2024 and *into* 2025, with some portion pushed further out to 2026 and beyond. Sivers' historical top line was worse than it appeared; its current period looks marginally better partly as an artifact of that reallocation.

## The five levers — and which one cuts deepest

The company disclosed five specific restatement drivers. Taken in order of analytical importance:

**Development capitalization impairment** is the most consequential. Swedish K3 accounting allows companies to capitalise R&D spending as a balance-sheet asset when commercial viability is assessed as probable. PCAOB applies a stricter standard: the threshold for recognising such capitalised costs is higher, and absent sufficient commercial evidence — signed volume commitments, for instance, rather than letters of intent — the asset must be expensed. Sivers had capitalised meaningful development expenditures under K3. The PCAOB restatement effectively says: not yet. The SEK 127-million reduction in book equity is the cumulative balance-sheet footprint of this reclassification. For a company whose equity coverage story depends heavily on the asset base supporting its laser platform, the haircut is not trivial.

**Revenue reallocation between periods** is conceptually simpler but historically damaging. Under PCAOB revenue recognition standards, certain contracts or milestone payments that K3 had recognised in FY2024 did not yet meet the criteria for recognition. The result is a FY2024 revenue revision from SEK 243.7M down to SEK 219.2M — a reduction of SEK 24.5 million, or roughly 10% of what was reported. More strikingly, the FY2024 net loss was revised from SEK 116.3M to SEK 183.9M — a SEK 67.6 million widening. Investors who benchmarked Sivers' loss trajectory against the K3 numbers have been working from a flattering baseline. The underlying deterioration in FY2024 was substantially larger than reported.

**Inventory revaluation** and **share-based compensation fair value updates** are more mechanical in nature. Inventory write-downs under PCAOB's lower-of-cost-or-net-realisable-value tests tend to be applied more conservatively than under K3; the fair value methodology for equity-settled awards follows US GAAP conventions that can produce different expense recognition patterns. Neither driver is unusual in a dual-listing restatement context. Both add to the cumulative EBIT drag.

**Income statement reclassification from by-nature to by-function** reshapes presentation rather than outcomes — R&D, COGS, and G&A are recut so US-style investors can read gross margin and operating leverage directly. This does not change the total loss, but it changes how analysts model it.

## What five years of growth actually looks like

Strip away the accounting complexity and the underlying trajectory is real. Revenue has grown at a 36.7% CAGR from 2016 to 2025, a roughly 16x expansion over the decade, per analyst estimates at [Global Equity Briefing](https://www.globalequitybriefing.com/p/sivers-semiconductors-hype-or-asymmetric). Free cash outflow has narrowed from SEK 151 million in FY2022 to SEK 66 million in FY2025. Operating margin improved from -83% (FY2022) to -39% (FY2025). The direction of travel is correct. The absolute level remains heavily negative.

Q4 FY2025 standalone revenue of SEK 80.7M was up 5% year-on-year at reported rates, but 17% in constant currency — a divergence reflecting SEK appreciation. Product revenue of SEK 21.3M grew 13% quarter-on-quarter. The qualification-to-revenue lag in laser supply chains runs six to eighteen months from design-in to purchase order; Q4 product revenue is the seed of what may follow.

## Capital structure: the cost of survival

Sivers has funded its growth primarily through equity issuance. Since 2020, shares outstanding have increased by 101.58% — essentially, the share count doubled. Year-end FY2025 cash stood at SEK 43.5M against annual FCF consumption of SEK 66M: roughly three quarters of runway before the next financing event.

The recent financing sequence: a SEK 95M rights issue in 2025 (~8% dilution); a $17M refinancing with [Bootstrap Europe 4.0 S.à r.l.](https://news.cision.com/sivers-semiconductors/r/sivers-semiconductors-refinances-group-debt-facilities-with-bootstrap-europe-to-strengthen-capital-s,c4312725) on 24 February 2026 (split into a secured term loan and a $12M convertible at 10.85%); and a $6.6M non-dilutive NEMC Year 2 grant in May 2026. The convertible tranche carries embedded dilution optionality.

The June 15 AGM will ask shareholders to authorise the issuance of up to 53.8 million new shares — approximately 15% of current shares outstanding — plus a 2% long-term incentive plan. Management has cited four stated uses: organic growth funding, potential M&A, strategic shareholder onboarding, and US listing enablement. For a company that has doubled its share count in five years, any authorisation of this scope deserves scrutiny.

## The valuation arithmetic

At SEK 72.90 — a five-year high — Sivers' market capitalisation is approximately SEK 22.7 billion (~$2.2 billion). Against PCAOB-restated FY2025 revenue of SEK 306.6M, that is a price-to-sales multiple of approximately **74x**.

One analyst's bull-case 2030 model: 45% revenue CAGR, 25% operating margin, SEK 2.3 billion revenue, SEK 404 million net income — implying fair value of SEK 14.52 per share. The current price is roughly five times that estimate. The market is either assuming a considerably more aggressive ramp, a higher terminal margin, or pricing acquisition optionality. It is not pricing operational fundamentals as they currently exist.

## The frame for what follows

The PCAOB restatement resolves one question and opens another. The resolved question is which set of numbers an investor should use: the restated figures are the right baseline, and they show a company that lost SEK 222.6M on SEK 306.6M of revenue in FY2025. The open question is whether the narrative that justifies SEK 22.7B in market capitalisation — CPO production beginning end-2026, a $453M pipeline growing 64% year-on-year, a US listing that re-rates the stock against American comparables — will be validated by shipped product and cash-generating customer ramps, or whether it will dissolve under the weight of further dilution, delayed qualification timelines, and a laser market that is less concentrated than the bull case assumes.

The financials show a company that is **real** — the growth is there, the margin improvement is there, the pipeline has names attached to it. They also show a company that is **under-funded** for the ambition it is selling — three quarters of cash, a 15% dilution proposal, and a convertible overhang. And they show a company valued for a scenario that has **not yet shipped**. The chapters that follow examine the technology, the customer ramps, and the competitive position to assess whether that gap closes — or widens.

chapters.title: The five quarters that built the rally
chapters.body:
# The five quarters that built the rally

The stock spent most of 2023 and 2024 trading below SEK 5. Then it ran to SEK 72.90 — a 40-fold move from its five-year floor of SEK 1.80. The move demands explanation. Five quarters supply most of it.

## August 2024: the handover

The starting gun was quiet. On 19 August 2024, Vickram Vathulya replaced Anders Storm as CEO. Vathulya did not immediately change the financial trajectory, but he signalled a sharper commercial focus on co-packaged optics, repositioning the photonics narrative toward a specific upstream slot in the AI datacenter supply chain.

## H1 2025: rights issue and the quiet build

The first half of 2025 brought necessary but dilutive housekeeping. A SEK 95 million rights issue (~8% dilution) kept the balance sheet viable. Investor attention was migrating toward photonics, and toward what Sivers could mean for co-packaged optics specifically.

## September 29, 2025: the POET anchor

The inflection moment arrived at the end of the third quarter. Sivers and [POET Technologies](https://www.poet-technologies.com/news/poet-technologies-and-sivers-semiconductors-collaborate-on-external-light-sources-for-co-packaged-optics-and-next-generation-ai-market) announced a strategic collaboration to build External Light Source modules combining Sivers' high-power InP DFB lasers with POET's Optical Interposer platform. The deal contractually anchored Sivers' position in a specific CPO architecture at the moment CPO was becoming a central topic in AI infrastructure planning.

When Ayar Labs' SuperNova — a multi-wavelength light source using Sivers laser arrays, jointly demonstrated at ECOC 2022 — gained traction in specialist publications, the Sivers name travelled with it. The stock accelerated through Q4 2025.

## February 26, 2026: the preliminary read

The Q4 2025 preliminary results offered incremental validation: fourth-quarter net sales of SEK 80.7 million (5% reported, 17% constant FX), product revenue up 13% QoQ to SEK 21.3 million. Two days earlier, the company had disclosed the $17 million Bootstrap Europe refinancing — runway was still measured in months.

## May 13, 2026: the restatement that didn't crater anything

The annual report carried PCAOB-aligned restated financials. The revisions were not cosmetic (Chapter 4 details the mechanics), yet the stock barely moved — a data point about who now holds the shares. Institutional readers interpreted the restatement as accounting plumbing ahead of an SEC process, not operational deterioration.

## The MSCI trigger and the test ahead

Sivers joins the MSCI Sweden Small Cap Index effective 29 May 2026 — the same date Q1 2026 results are scheduled. Passive funds must buy regardless of what those results contain.

The rally has been built on genuine operational improvement, but what is not yet real is shipped CPO revenue. The POET ELS modules remain in early prototype phase, with production readiness targeted for end-2026. The unnamed LiDAR customer has a production ramp planned for Q4 2026. The next two to three quarters need to convert pipeline into production-stage revenue — not further partnership announcements. The thesis is coherent. The factory has not yet been asked to prove it.

chapters.title: The team that is going to ring the Nasdaq bell
chapters.body:
# The team that is going to ring the Nasdaq bell

## The architect and his timeline

The appointments did not arrive by coincidence. In August 2023, Bami Bastani joined as Strategic Advisor. By February 2024 he was Executive Chairman of the US subsidiary and Chairman of the Swedish parent. Six months later, a new CEO arrived. Eighteen months after that, the company filed PCAOB-aligned restated financials and nominated two new directors whose CVs read like a cross-border transaction checklist. The sequence is a programme.

Bastani is the architect. Forty-two years in semiconductors: component roles at Intel and National Semiconductor, systems-on-chip at Fujitsu Micro, then three separate tenures as a turnaround CEO at public companies — ANADIGICS, Trident Microsystems, and Meru Networks. Each required restructuring under quarterly earnings scrutiny. His final corporate role was Senior Vice President at GlobalFoundries, where he also served on the board of the Global Semiconductor Alliance. He is not a board ornament. He is the most experienced operating executive in the room, placed at the chairman seat to translate a Swedish mid-cap photonics company into something a Nasdaq roadshow can sell.

## The CEO who invested in his own bet

Vickram Vathulya was appointed President and CEO on 19 August 2024. His credentials are unusual for a Stockholm-listed company: PhD in Electrical Engineering from Lehigh, MBA from Berkeley Haas, twenty-five years in semiconductors. At NXP he ran RF and wireless business lines; at Maxim Integrated he grew the RF portfolio and revitalised the standard products division. His most recent pre-Sivers role was President of Nuvotronics, where he led a strategic transformation.

What distinguishes the appointment is the share commitment: up to two million Sivers shares, a personal commitment valued at up to $1 million. A Lehigh PhD and Berkeley MBA running a Swedish-listed compound semiconductor company is staffed for a Nasdaq investor day, not European institutional comfort. (His framing of the POET partnership — "a highly complementary fit between our high-performance DFB lasers and POET's innovative optical interposer platform" — has become the most-quoted line in specialist commentary; the collaboration is mapped in Chapter 7.)

## The door was already open

Todd Thomson joined the Sivers board in 2021, three years before Bastani arrived. That sequence matters: Thomson did not follow Bastani onto the board. He preceded him.

His CV is the most concentrated source of US capital-markets credibility on the board: MBA from Wharton, CFO of Citigroup for five years, CEO of Citigroup Global Wealth Management (~$10 billion division), CEO of Citigroup Alternative Investments, chair of the Citi Pension Investment Committee. Before Citi, his career ran through Bain, Booz Allen, GE Capital, and advisory work at GlobalFoundries. He currently serves as COO and CFO of Kairos Ventures.

A former Citi CFO does not join a Stockholm small-cap for passive oversight. Thomson, in all probability, was the figure who opened the door.

## The technical floor

Karin Raj, CTO Europe at Nokia, carries direct operational authority in the exact intersection of domains Sivers sells into: telecommunications, satellite communications, semiconductors, photonics. Her career has taken her through Ericsson and across geographies including the US, China, India, France, Turkey and the Nordics. She led technical functions through multiple wireless-generation transitions.

At Sivers she chairs the Investment Committee — the board subcommittee with authority over capital expenditure decisions. For a company whose central thesis rests on InP DFB lasers being irreplaceable upstream, having a sitting Nokia CTO Europe making the capex calls is the credibility mechanism that keeps the roadmap honest.

## The departures are not symmetrical

Fällström leaves the board alongside two other directors: Tomas Duffy and Keith Halsey. The three departures are not equivalent.

Tomas Duffy is the institutional memory. He joined in 2016, became Chairman in 2018, and was present at every major structural decision: the 2017 CST Global acquisition, the 2022 MixComm acquisition, and the rebrand. His pre-Sivers career at EKN Exportkreditnämnden — the Swedish state export credit agency — anchored European institutional credibility through the growth-stage years. The transition to a US-listing-architect chairman made him surplus to the next phase rather than wrong for the previous one.

Erik Fällström's departure is different in character. He is a co-founder, CEO of DDM Debt, and controls approximately 11.8% of Sivers' voting rights through DDM and the Fällström Family Office — a stake he retains after leaving the board. DDM has publicly stated it wishes to drive Sivers "toward a broader investment company," a strategic vision in direct tension with the focused-operating-company narrative a Nasdaq listing requires. His departure clears the room for a US roadshow story; his continuing economic stake means the strategic tension relocates to the shareholder register.

Keith Halsey was elected at the 15 May 2024 AGM and departs approximately thirteen months later. He was Chairman of CST Global before its 2017 acquisition. His rotation completes the unwinding of the original CST acquisition cohort from the board.

## The incoming slate

Joakim Nideborn, nominated as Vice Chairman, is the sitting CFO and Deputy CEO of HMS Networks AB, a Nasdaq Stockholm-listed industrial communications company. His stated focus at Sivers is primary oversight of the board for Nordic-region customers, employees and investors — the governance counterpart to Bastani's US-capital-markets orientation.

Helena Svancar spent ten years at Deutsche Bank rising to Managing Director and Head of Corporate Finance Nordics, then nearly five years as Head of M&A at Ericsson before joining Verdane as a Partner in September 2022. She currently serves as a non-executive director at Onomondo and Truecaller (chairing the Remuneration Committee). A former Deutsche Bank Head of Corporate Finance Nordics and former Ericsson M&A chief is the addition a board makes when it expects to execute cross-border transactions.

## Overhang

Two concurrent governance concerns shadow the AGM. Sweden's Ekobrottsmyndigheten is examining possible market abuse violations connected to the Nasdaq dual-listing announcement, which leaked approximately forty-eight hours early via an anonymous account on X. The investigation is open as of the snapshot date. Separately, Sivers joins the MSCI Sweden Small Cap Index on 29 May 2026 — the same date Q1 results land under PCAOB. That is an unusual collision of technical and fundamental catalysts.

## The shape of the board

Post-AGM, the board numbers five: Bastani as Executive Chairman, Vathulya as CEO, Nideborn as Vice Chairman with Nordic-governance oversight, Thomson as the US capital-markets anchor, Raj as Investment Committee chair, and Svancar adding M&A capability.

The Swedish founder-investor presence is being cleared out. The shape that remains says Nasdaq New York. Four of the five directors carry primary professional identities in corporate-finance and transactional execution. The only question the board composition leaves open is timing.

chapters.title: Where Sivers sits in the AI photonics stack
chapters.body:
# Where Sivers sits in the AI photonics stack

## The layer that doesn't ship to hyperscalers

Investors sometimes speak as though Sivers has a direct line into hyperscaler procurement. It does not. Understanding where Sivers actually sits in the stack is the single most analytically productive exercise in evaluating the $453 million pipeline.

The CPO supply chain runs in layers. At the top sit the hyperscalers: Microsoft, Meta, AWS, Google. Below them are GPU and accelerator vendors — NVIDIA, AMD, Marvell, Broadcom. Below that is the critical integration layer: CPO module integrators — POET Technologies, Ayar Labs, Lightmatter, Lightelligence, Celestial AI — whose job is to assemble optical interposers and ELS modules. It is at this layer that the laser question becomes urgent. And it is here, one rung below, that Sivers operates.

Sivers Photonics manufactures InP DFB lasers and laser arrays that ship to the design houses at the CPO integration layer. Those design houses are the gatekeepers. Whether Sivers' chokepoint position converts to revenue depends entirely on which of its design-house customers wins which hyperscaler design slot.

## POET: the most consequential named partnership

On 29 September 2025, Sivers and [POET Technologies](https://www.poet-technologies.com/news/poet-technologies-and-sivers-semiconductors-collaborate-on-external-light-sources-for-co-packaged-optics-and-next-generation-ai-market) announced a strategic collaboration to develop ELS modules for CPO and the broader AI infrastructure market. POET brings the integration substrate (its Optical Interposer platform); Sivers brings the laser. The target market, per analyst Tim Savageaux, is a $1 billion-plus annual ELS market, sitting inside a broader AI optical connectivity opportunity estimated above $50 billion.

Early prototypes are targeted for H1 2026; production readiness for end-2026. POET is a small-cap stock (NASDAQ/TSX) with its own execution risk. The partnership is real — the product roadmap is aspirational until hardware ships at yield.

## Ayar Labs: the longer, quieter relationship

The Ayar relationship predates the current CPO investment cycle. At ECOC 2022, Sivers and Ayar jointly showcased DFB laser arrays integrated into Ayar's SuperNova multi-wavelength light source — the optical engine at the centre of Ayar's hyperscale AI interconnect proposition. The SuperNova is widely regarded as one of the most technically advanced commercial CPO light-source candidates.

The Ayar relationship matters for two reasons. First, it is a multi-year demonstrated supplier arrangement, not a press-release bilateral. Second, if Ayar wins a design slot with a major hyperscaler, Sivers laser arrays are plausibly inside that win. That indirect exposure is analytically real — though Sivers has not confirmed it as a customer relationship.

## O-Net/Enablence and the thermal constraint

The third named design-house customer is O-Net Communications, working through its Enablence Technologies subsidiary on ELS modules with integrated thermal solutions for CPO. Thermal management is critical: yield loss at thermal qualification is one of the primary reasons CPO module production has not yet scaled. O-Net as a mid-cap Chinese company carries geopolitical and commercial risks that any investor building a western-supply-chain thesis should weigh.

## imec: the structural endorsement

Sivers established a joint development programme with imec — Belgium's microelectronics research consortium and the European reference centre for silicon photonics — beginning in 2019. The collaboration integrates C-band InP DFB lasers onto imec's silicon photonics platform. A seven-year integration collaboration with imec is a better proxy for the maturity of Sivers' laser technology than any individual commercial press release.

## The wireless and defence customers: a different revenue profile

The European Space Agency and Intelsat are named customers for millimetre-wave beamformer hardware. The $6.6 million NEMC Year 2 grant supports domestic defence electronics infrastructure.

The single largest disclosed revenue potential sits with an unnamed automotive LiDAR customer deploying Sivers technology "across all their platforms" — lifecycle revenue estimated at $53–138 million over eight to ten years. Production is projected for Q4 2026.

## Concentration risk and the pipeline caveat

The $453 million pipeline is distributed across named partnerships and undisclosed parties. No single customer exceeds 25% of that figure.

The analytical problem: POET is a small-cap with its own funding pressures. Ayar Labs is private and pre-revenue at hyperscaler scale. O-Net carries cross-border risk. The entire commercial layer that Sivers supplies is itself in early-stage commercialisation. A pipeline distributed across customers who are not yet at scale is not the same as a pipeline distributed across customers shipping at volume.

The implied indirect exposure — to Marvell (via Celestial AI), AMD, Lightmatter, Lightelligence — is structural optionality, not disclosed revenue exposure. Sivers has not confirmed any of these as direct customer relationships.

## The validation test

If NVIDIA, Microsoft, Meta, or Amazon were to name Sivers — directly or via one of its design-house customers in a hyperscale optical-interconnect announcement — the supply-chain position would convert from technically plausible to commercially validated. As of 23 May 2026, none of this has happened.

Sivers' chokepoint is real in a narrow technical sense: there are very few independent western InP DFB laser foundries with the combination of C-band performance, power density, and volume capability that CPO demands. But scarcity is a necessary condition for pricing power, not a sufficient one. Whether the chokepoint translates into revenue depends on decisions being made one layer above Sivers. The company is the right answer to a question the market is still deciding whether to ask.

chapters.title: Why the comparison is COHR and LITE, but the analog is something smaller
chapters.body:
# Why the comparison is COHR and LITE, but the analog is something smaller

## The scale gap is not the point

The instinct to benchmark against American-listed incumbents leads to Coherent Corp. (COHR) and Lumentum (LITE) — two companies that in March 2026 received a combined $2 billion each in simultaneous strategic investments from NVIDIA.

The size comparison is arresting. Coherent's annualised run-rate exceeds $7 billion. Lumentum tracks above $3 billion. MACOM generates approximately $700 million. Sivers reported FY2025 net sales of approximately $33 million. By revenue, this is a David-and-skyscraper story.

That framing, however, mistakes the competitive question. Sivers is not competing for Coherent's transceiver integration business. It is positioned at a specific, narrow layer that is structurally reorganising as the industry migrates from pluggable transceivers toward co-packaged optics.

## What changes at the CPO layer

In pluggable transceiver architecture, lasers are commoditised within standard form factors. The large integrated players and Japanese generics (Furukawa Electric, Sumitomo Electric) are optimised for this world — volume, cost efficiency, yield across millions of units.

Co-packaged optics disrupts this. When lasers move into the package itself — directly adjacent to switch silicon — specification requirements diverge from any standard catalogue. Each customer's interposer geometry, thermal envelope, channel count, and wavelength grid is bespoke. Sivers emphasises "customised III-V lasers for specific customer specifications" — language mapping precisely to what POET, Ayar Labs, and O-Net require. Whether that custom-specification layer carries durable pricing power against the integrated giants' resources is the open question.

## The counterargument has substance

Both integrated giants are expanding InP capacity faster than the chokepoint thesis would prefer. Coherent doubled 6-inch InP wafer output one quarter ahead of schedule. Lumentum has acquired a fifth InP fabrication facility in Greensboro, North Carolina. These are not the moves of companies that have ceded the high-specification layer.

## The real comparable: MACOM, not Coherent

The more instructive competitive frame is MACOM Technology Solutions — a publicly traded laser-chip pure-play with explicit CPO laser supply positioning, not attempting to compete in transceiver assembly.

| Company | Annual Revenue | Market Cap | Revenue Multiple |
|---|---|---|---|
| Coherent (COHR) | ~$7.2B | ~$19B | ~2.6× |
| Lumentum (LITE) | ~$3.2B | ~$8B | ~2.5× |
| MACOM | ~$700M | ~$10B | ~14× |
| **Sivers Semiconductors** | **~$33M** | **~$2.2B** | **~67×** |

At ~67x revenue, Sivers would need to multiply its top line approximately 20x to reach MACOM's run-rate. The gap to the analyst bull-case fair value (SEK 14.52) suggests investors are pricing a scenario considerably more aggressive — or pricing acquisition optionality before any acquirer has emerged.

## Geography as an unpriced variable

From the perspective of a hyperscaler constructing a CPO supply chain under conditions of US-China technology bifurcation and East Asian supply concentration risk, a European-headquartered independent InP laser source has structural value that does not appear in a DCF model. The $6.6 million NEMC Year 2 grant is consistent with the thesis that Western government entities view Sivers as a strategic supply option.

## The historical pattern, and what it requires

The competitive template Sivers' investment thesis borrows is well-established. EML laser specialists who captured the 100G-to-400G transceiver transition built the design-win foundation that became Lumentum's franchise. Applied Optoelectronics captured disproportionate upside in the 800G and 1.6T cycle during 2025 by being the right-size, right-specification supplier at the precise moment hyperscalers were racing to lock up supply.

Sivers is positioned at the equivalent inflection for CPO DFB lasers. The preconditions for execution are demanding: a named hyperscaler production order, a successful fab ramp from Glasgow, and a financing structure that avoids forced dilution before revenue arrives.

The competitive position is asymmetric. Sivers can lose if the integrated giants expand custom-laser capability faster than CPO adoption creates lock-in, or if a hyperscaler decides the laser layer is too strategic to outsource. Sivers wins disproportionately only if one of the POET, Ayar, or O-Net partnerships converts to a named hyperscaler production order before the window narrows. The current market price already assumes a version of that outcome — leaving limited room for the execution risk the financials are signalling.

chapters.title: Twelve months of headlines + how the equity story has traveled in specialist commentary
chapters.body:
# Twelve months of headlines — and how the equity story has travelled

## The leadership shift that reframed the company

When Sivers replaced Anders Storm with Vickram Vathulya in August 2024, the market took limited notice. The stock was trading below SEK 10. What the appointment signalled — a pivot toward a sharper commercial thesis built around co-packaged optics — would take another year to register in price.

## The POET partnership and the re-rating

Then, on 29 September 2025, came the announcement that repriced the equity story: the [POET Technologies](https://www.poet-technologies.com/news/poet-technologies-and-sivers-semiconductors-collaborate-on-external-light-sources-for-co-packaged-optics-and-next-generation-ai-market) collaboration. The market did not wait for shipped revenue: the stock accelerated sharply through Q4 2025 as the CPO pure-play thesis consolidated around Sivers as the InP laser foundry that neither POET, Ayar Labs, nor O-Net can replicate internally.

## February 2026: the refinancing

On 24 February, Sivers announced the [Bootstrap Europe](https://news.cision.com/sivers-semiconductors/r/sivers-semiconductors-refinances-group-debt-facilities-with-bootstrap-europe-to-strengthen-capital-s,c4312725) refinancing. Two days later, Q4 preliminary results landed.

## The restatement: tighter accounting, wider losses

The fuller reckoning came on [13 May 2026](https://www.sivers-semiconductors.com/press/sivers-semiconductors-publishes-the-2025-annual-report-adjusting-prior-reported-financials-as-preparation-for-a-potential-dual-listing-in-the-united-states/), when Sivers published a PCAOB-aligned Annual Report. The mechanics are dissected in Chapter 4.

## May 2026: grants, governance, and an open investigation

Six days after the annual report, Sivers announced the $6.6 million [NEMC Year 2 grant](https://www.sivers-semiconductors.com/investors/). Board nominations for the June 15 AGM followed on May 20. The Ekobrottsmyndigheten insider-trading investigation remains open.

Forward catalysts within 90-180 days: Q1 2026 results (delayed at snapshot), the June 15 AGM, a potential Nasdaq dual-listing announcement, and the POET prototype demonstration. Into H2 2026-2027: POET production readiness and the unnamed LiDAR customer's ramp in Q4 2026. None of these has been de-risked.

## How the equity story has travelled in specialist commentary

The stock's 40x move from its SEK 1.80 five-year low to SEK 72.90 has generated sustained retail attention on X/Twitter. The account @aleabitoreddit has published approximately 385 posts on Sivers across 2025-2026.

One widely-followed commentator has pattern-matched Sivers to Lumentum's 2024 trajectory — positioning this as the moment LITE occupied before hyperscaler design-in announcements triggered a re-rating. The comparison is structurally consistent, but the timing depends on announcements that have not yet occurred. The POET collaboration is the nearest thing to named-hyperscaler adjacency in the public record. Until a production design win is confirmed, the chokepoint thesis remains a bet on supply-chain position, not a validated order book.

chapters.title: InP DFB lasers — patents, products, and the case for chokepoint pricing
chapters.body:
# InP DFB lasers — patents, products, and the case for chokepoint pricing

The IP density question is the right place to start. If Sivers holds a genuine chokepoint, it commands pricing power and customer stickiness. If sufficiently motivated competitors can replicate its process within a product cycle, it's simply a modestly sized fabricator with a temporarily favorable order book.

Public patent databases show Sivers Photonics holding three issued patents and 16 applications pending across US, UK, Canada, and WIPO jurisdictions. The USPTO has issued patents including *Distributed feedback laser having enhanced etch stop features* and *Method of making an InP-based DFB laser* — both signalling process-level IP rather than end-product claims.

Coherent and Lumentum each hold hundreds of issued laser patents. Measured by count, Sivers' 19 total filings look thin. But that comparison misfires — those portfolios were built around volume production of standard telecom lasers, not continuous-wave InP DFB designs optimized for silicon photonics integration in the C-band (1530–1565nm) window required for CPO.

## The three-layer technical stack

The chokepoint isn't a single component — it's the integrated capability to execute across three distinct technical disciplines simultaneously.

First, III-V epitaxial growth: indium phosphide is grown in MBE or MOCVD systems where tolerances are measured in fractions of a percent. Most university labs can grow InP; very few do so at device-grade quality for high-power telecom applications. Second, DFB grating fabrication: etching gratings at nanometer-scale periodicity into InP requires electron-beam lithography and process consistency to produce predictable wavelengths across a wafer. Third, InP-on-silicon-photonics integration: attaching an InP die to a silicon photonics waveguide introduces mode mismatch, thermal expansion differences, and alignment tolerances.

Sivers' collaboration with [imec](https://www.imec-int.com/) addresses this third layer directly. Imec is the European reference centre for silicon photonics process development; its decision to use Sivers as the laser-supply partner is a structural third-party endorsement.

## Where the patents don't tell the whole story

Three issued patents is a narrow disclosed moat. What matters more, in specialty semiconductor fabrication, is trade-secret process know-how — the exact MOCVD conditions, dopant profiles, passivation chemistry — which exists in process control systems, not patent filings. The rational strategy is to patent the most obvious design-arounds and protect the rest as trade secrets.

The accumulated process knowledge of the Glasgow fab represents more than a decade of continuous development that can't be easily reconstructed. The counterargument: trade-secret moats erode when engineers move. A well-funded competitor could, in principle, hire the relevant process staff and rebuild the capability within three to five years.

## R&D intensity, obscured by accounting

Sivers doesn't publish a clean R&D expense line. The PCAOB restatement added a nuance: among its drivers was the "impairment of previously capitalised development expenditures" — R&D costs written off as current-period expenses under US GAAP rather than spread forward. Reported earnings will be depressed through the entire investment phase.

## The margin horizon

Whether the IP and process investment generates returns depends on production volume sufficient to spread fab fixed costs across enough units to drive operating leverage.

[MACOM Technology Solutions](https://www.macom.com/) has historically achieved operating margins above 20% in its photonics business. MACOM's margin profile is the destination; Sivers' -39% is the departure point. The distance between them is measured in customer production ramps.

The continuation of the NEMC Year 2 grant implies technical milestones were met on the military-application side — limited evidence of execution credibility, but evidence nonetheless.

The IP moat is best understood not as a patent count but as a combination: three fabrication disciplines integrated in a single facility, a decade-plus of process knowledge, and collaborative relationships that impose switching costs on the demand side. Whether that constitutes a durable chokepoint or a temporary technical lead is what the next two years of customer ramps will determine.

chapters.title: What could break this
chapters.body:
# What could break this

The bull case rests on a sequence: two production ramps both hit their 2026 targets, the $453M pipeline converts to revenue faster than dilution compounds, and a US Nasdaq listing unlocks capital needed to cross operating breakeven. Disrupt any single link — and the timeline for profitability slides into 2028 or beyond.

## The calendar problem

Both highest-stakes production milestones fall within a seven-to-nine month window from the snapshot date. The [POET collaboration](https://www.sivers-semiconductors.com/) targets production-readiness by end-2026. The unnamed LiDAR customer is targeting a Q4 2026 production ramp.

Semiconductor production ramps do not routinely hit first-announced dates. A two-quarter slip in either program would not merely delay revenue recognition; it would compress the operating margin improvement trajectory that underpins consensus for a 2027 EBIT crossover. The company has demonstrated directional improvement; it has not demonstrated an ability to execute a simultaneous dual production ramp.

## The runway equation

At year-end 2025, Sivers held SEK 43.5M in cash against FCF of approximately -SEK 66M. Each financing injection extends the runway; none resolves the structural equation.

The June 15 AGM includes authorization to issue up to 15% of shares. That headroom request is not neutral: boards seek dilution authority because they expect to use it.

## A pipeline is not a backlog

The $453M pipeline is the most-cited metric. The named counterparties — POET, Ayar Labs, O-Net, and the LiDAR customer — each represent multi-quarter design wins, not purchase orders.

Design wins can be withdrawn. If the automotive customer — the single largest disclosed lifecycle exposure — exits before volumes begin, the pipeline headline would fall materially, and with it the multiple current shareholders have priced in. The $453M number is a probability-weighted projection over a decade-long horizon. No conversion rate has yet been established by results.

## The chokepoint is closing

The strategic logic depends on large integrated players not replicating InP DFB laser capacity quickly enough to displace Sivers from new design wins. That assumption is under active pressure. Coherent doubled InP wafer output one quarter ahead of schedule. Lumentum acquired a fifth InP fab. Most consequentially, NVIDIA committed $2 billion each to COHR and LITE in March 2026 — capital injections explicitly targeting the capacity bottleneck that defines Sivers' position.

If their capacity expansions close the chokepoint before Sivers completes its production ramp and locks in design wins, pricing leverage and design-win capture rate both weaken simultaneously.

## What the restatement signals

Chapter 4 dissects the PCAOB mechanics; the risk-specific question is whether the disclosed adjustments are bounded. If further PCAOB review surfaces additional adjustments — particularly in revenue recognition or R&D capitalisation — the listing could be delayed or downsized.

## The overhang that stays

Co-founder Erik Fällström departs the board, but his economic stake (~11.8% of votes via DDM Debt) remains intact. DDM has publicly stated it wants to drive Sivers toward a "broader investment company" — a direction incompatible with the focused operating-company narrative a US roadshow requires. His removal from governance eliminates one source of friction; his continued shareholding preserves the optionality to reassert it.

The Ekobrottsmyndigheten is investigating market abuse related to the listing announcement, which leaked approximately 48 hours early. An adverse finding would feature in the listing prospectus — giving US institutional investors a documented reason to pass.

Finally, the currency exposure is structural. Q4 2025 revenue grew 5% reported but 17% constant FX — a 12-percentage-point gap. A company pitching a Nasdaq listing on SEK-reported numbers is asking investors to build their own FX model.

chapters.title: Three events that will decide whether the rally was right
chapters.body:
# Three events that will decide whether the rally was right

## The vote that clears the table

On June 15, Sivers shareholders will gather to approve a board reshuffled for a single purpose: making the company legible to American institutional capital. Three seats empty; two are being filled by Joakim Nideborn (proposed as Vice Chairman) and Helena Svancar. (Chapter 6 carries the leadership map in full.)

The procedural outcome is not in doubt. What *is* in doubt is institutional sentiment around the dilution authority that accompanies the reshuffle: shareholders will vote to authorize issuance of up to 53.8 million new shares (~15% of the float), usable for organic growth, M&A, or a US listing capital raise.

The complicating factor is the open Ekobrottsmyndigheten investigation. An AGM that produces the expected board outcome while leaving that matter unresolved does not close the overhang — it merely defers it.

## The module that must ship

The POET partnership is the structural argument for the entire chokepoint thesis in a single press release. Timeline on paper: early prototypes in H1 2026; production readiness by end-2026. What the timeline cannot capture is module yield rates, thermal performance in sustained operation, and — most critically — named hyperscaler design-in. None of those have been publicly confirmed.

A successful production launch with a named hyperscaler in Q4 2026 would validate the upstream laser-chokepoint model. A two-quarter slip shifts production validation into mid-2027 — by which time Sivers will almost certainly have exercised at least a portion of its new dilution authority.

## The price that sets the ceiling

The PCAOB restatement was a prerequisite. The AGM dilution authority is the issuance vehicle. The MSCI inclusion provides a passive-buying tailwind. What remains is the actual listing announcement and the price at which Sivers raises US dollars.

At SEK 72.90 and 311.3 million shares, the market capitalises Sivers at roughly SEK 22.7 billion (~$2.2 billion) against PCAOB-restated FY2025 revenue of SEK 306.6 million — a P/S multiple of approximately 74×. One analyst's 2030 bull case arrives at a fair value of SEK 14.52. The gap implies the market is pricing a ramp materially more aggressive than the published bull case supports.

If Sivers prices a US offering at or above SEK 60, it validates the current equity story. If it prices materially below, the share price has limited support above the offering level.

The bull case requires POET prototypes on schedule in H1 2026, production with a named customer in Q4, FY2026 revenue above SEK 450 million, and an operating loss that narrows below SEK 100 million. The bear case does not require a disaster — only a two-quarter delay.

The next 18 months will determine whether the chokepoint is real — or simply early-stage.

chapters.title: Appendices
chapters.body:
The tables and reference materials that follow are organised to let readers pressure-test the arguments made in the preceding chapters against the underlying numbers and primary sources.

## Financial Tables

The financial appendix presents three years of income-statement and balance-sheet data in parallel columns — Swedish K3 as filed and PCAOB-restated — so the SEK 36.5M gap in FY2025 EBIT (–141.3M reported vs. –177.8M restated) and the FY2024 revenue compression (243.7M → 219.2M) are visible at a glance alongside the five restatement drivers.

## Leadership Graph

The leadership appendix maps board tenure, departure dates, and the professional lineage connecting Vickram Vathulya, Bami Bastani, and the incoming AGM nominees — tracing the organisational logic of the US-listing preparation from the August 2023 strategic advisor appointment through the June 2026 board reshuffle.

## Counterparty Map

The counterparty appendix organises named partners, named customers, implied indirect customers, and creditors into a single reference table, with segment, scope, and confirmation status flagged for each relationship.

## Press Release Index

Chronological index of material company announcements from 2023 through the snapshot date, with direct links.

## Aleabit Primary-Source Notes

Raw excerpts and commentary from the Aleabit research thread that surfaced several claims — including the Apple/SiPH reference — not yet confirmed in official Sivers filings. Treat as unverified leads.

DDM has publicly flagged that it 'wants to drive the company towards a broader investment company' — a vision in direct tension with the operational-focus thesis of the US-listing prep. His departure clears the room for a Nasdaq pitch that needs to talk about Sivers as a focused operating company, not as a vehicle for an activist holding play.

departing_at_2026_06_15_agm.name: Tomas Duffy
departing_at_2026_06_15_agm.education: BSc, Kungliga tekniska högskolan (Royal Institute of Technology, KTH), 1976-1980
career: Director of Large Corporates + Head of Telecom, EKN Exportkreditnämnden (Swedish Export Credit Agency), Dec 2010 - April 2017
Sivers IMA / Sivers Semiconductors Chair (since 2018; now Vice Chairman pre-departure)
departing_at_2026_06_15_agm.framing: Duffy is the institutional memory. He joined the board in 2016, became chairman in 2018, and was at the table for the 2017 CST Global acquisition, the 2022 MixComm acquisition, and the Sivers IMA → Sivers Semiconductors rebrand. His pre-Sivers career — Swedish state export-credit telecom finance — anchored the European institutional credibility of the entity through the early growth-stage years. The transition to a US-listing-architect chairman (Bastani) made him surplus to the next phase rather than wrong for the previous one.

departing_at_2026_06_15_agm.name: Keith Halsey
departing_at_2026_06_15_agm.framing: Halsey served only ~13 months before this reshuffle (elected May 2024, departing June 2026). Public biographical detail remains thin in the sources reviewed at the snapshot date — flag as a genuine sourcing gap and not a basis for inference. The short tenure pattern is consistent with a transitional appointment between the pre-Bastani board and the US-listing-prep board, but the rationale for his rotation is not stated in the AGM materials.

continuing_directors.name: Todd Thomson
continuing_directors.title: Independent Director (since 2021)
continuing_directors.education: MBA Wharton; BA Economics Davidson College
career: Citigroup Global Wealth Management — CEO ($10B division, 2.5 years)
Currently: COO & CFO, Kairos Ventures (US VC firm)
Investment Committees: Dynasty, Davidson College, World Resources Institute
continuing_directors.significance: Thomson is the most credentialed US-capital-markets figure on the board — former Citi CFO, former CEO of Citi's $10B Global Wealth Management division. He joined Sivers in 2021, three years before Bastani arrived and four years before the PCAOB restatement. He is therefore not part of the US-listing wave of appointments; he is the figure who LIKELY OPENED THE DOOR to the US-listing thesis in the first place. The Bastani-Vathulya-Thomson combination is unusually heavy on US public-company experience for a Swedish small-cap and that concentration is deliberate.

continuing_directors.name: Karin Raj
continuing_directors.title: Independent, Non-executive Board Director; Chair, Investment Committee
continuing_directors.sivers_role: Chair of the Investment Committee — structural authority over capex decisions
continuing_directors.framing: Raj is the technical anchor of the board. As Nokia's CTO Europe she carries direct big-tech-company experience in the exact intersection of segments Sivers operates in (telecom + satcom + semiconductors + photonics). Her chair of the Investment Committee role is the closest thing on the Sivers board to a structural CTO function — independent technical review of capex and product roadmap decisions.

new_nominees_2026_06_15_agm.name: Joakim Nideborn
new_nominees_2026_06_15_agm.background: Broad experience as CFO at listed technology companies
new_nominees_2026_06_15_agm.stated_focus: Primary oversight of the Board for customers, employees, and investors in the Nordic region
new_nominees_2026_06_15_agm.current_role: CFO and Deputy CEO, HMS Networks AB (Nasdaq Stockholm listed industrial communications)
new_nominees_2026_06_15_agm.framing: Nideborn is a SITTING listed-company CFO and Deputy CEO at HMS Networks — a Nasdaq Stockholm industrial communications company. He is not a 'broad CFO background' in the abstract; he is a working CFO at a comparable Swedish listed tech company. The Vice Chairman role at Sivers gives him primary oversight of Nordic-region customers, employees, and investors — the governance counterpart to Bastani's US-capital-markets orientation.

new_nominees_2026_06_15_agm.name: Helena Svancar
new_nominees_2026_06_15_agm.background: More than 20 years of international leadership experience
new_nominees_2026_06_15_agm.current_role: Partner, Verdane (Nordic growth-equity firm), since September 2022
career: Deutsche Bank — last 10 years; Managing Director and Head of Corporate Finance Nordics
Ericsson — Head of M&A for nearly 5 years
new_nominees_2026_06_15_agm.education: CEMS MSc in Finance and International Management — Stockholm School of Economics + University of St. Gallen
concurrent_boards: Truecaller — Non-Executive Director; Chair of Remuneration Committee
new_nominees_2026_06_15_agm.framing: Svancar is the most cross-border M&A-pedigreed director on the Sivers board. She was Head of M&A at Ericsson for nearly five years — running the M&A desk at one of Sweden's most acquisitive large-cap tech companies — and before that spent a decade at Deutsche Bank rising to Managing Director and Head of Corporate Finance Nordics. Her appointment to a board preparing a US dual listing is signal-dense: a former Deutsche Bank Head of Corporate Finance Nordics and former Ericsson M&A head is the addition a board makes when it expects to execute cross-border transactions.

post_agm_board_composition.framing: 5-person board (vs Unitika's 12-person director+auditor structure) reflects Swedish corporate governance norms. Smaller boards are typical for growth-stage Swedish-listed companies; smaller boards are also typical for companies preparing US listings where the SEC + NYSE/Nasdaq corporate governance rules emphasize majority-independent + audit-committee + governance-committee structures.

concurrent_governance_concerns.insider_trading_investigation: Sweden's Economic Crime Authority (Ekobrottsmyndigheten) is examining possible market abuse violations related to the Nasdaq listing announcement, which leaked roughly 48 hours early via an anonymous X account. The investigation is open as of the snapshot date and the outcome could materially affect investor sentiment heading into the AGM.
concurrent_governance_concerns.msci_inclusion_timing: Sivers joins MSCI Sweden Small Cap Index on 2026-05-29 — the same day Q1 results are released (delayed from earlier window) — forcing passive fund buying simultaneously with the first earnings under the new PCAOB regime.

leadership.board_composition_observation: The post-AGM board carries FOUR directors whose primary professional identity is corporate-finance and M&A execution: Bastani (3× public-company turnaround CEO), Thomson (ex-Citi CFO, current Kairos COO/CFO), Nideborn (sitting HMS Networks CFO + Deputy CEO), and Svancar (ex-Deutsche Bank Head of Corporate Finance Nordics + ex-Ericsson Head of M&A). For a Stockholm small-cap that is approximately $2.2B market cap, this concentration of corporate-finance pedigree is unusually heavy and points to a board built not just for organic growth but for transactional work — the planned US dual listing being the explicit case, acquisitions to scale up before listing being an obvious adjacency.

counterparties.headline: Sivers is the upstream chokepoint in the AI co-packaged optics (CPO) supply chain — supplying DFB lasers and laser arrays to the design houses (POET, Ayar Labs, O-Net) that assemble the External Light Source (ELS) and optical interposer modules that hyperscaler customers integrate into their next-generation GPU packages. The customer ecosystem reaches Marvell (via Celestial AI), AAPL (SiPH for consumer devices), AMD, Jabil, Lightmatter, and Lightelligence indirectly. Direct named customer wins to date: POET, Ayar Labs, O-Net/Enablence, an unnamed automotive LiDAR customer ('across all their platforms'), European Space Agency, and Intelsat.

named_partnerships.scope: External Light Source (ELS) modules for Co-Packaged Optics and next-generation AI infrastructure. Combines Sivers' high-power DFB lasers with POET's Optical Interposer platform.
named_partnerships.timeline: Early prototypes H1 2026; production readiness end-2026
named_partnerships.market_estimate: $1B+ annual ELS market (per analyst Tim Savageaux); broader AI optical connectivity market >$50B
named_partnerships.ceo_quote_sivers: We see a highly complementary fit between our high-performance DFB lasers and POET's innovative optical interposer platform. — Vickram Vathulya
named_partnerships.ceo_quote_poet: Modules optimized for size, performance and cost – exactly what the CPO and AI markets demand. — Dr. Suresh Venkatesan, POET Executive Chairman & CEO

named_partnerships.scope: Sivers provides DFB laser arrays for Ayar Labs' SuperNova multi-wavelength light source. Demonstrated together at ECOC 2022.
named_partnerships.significance: Ayar is one of the leading optical interconnect IP companies for AI hyperscale; its SuperNova is the optical engine that may go into the next generation of AI accelerator packages.

named_partnerships.scope: ELS modules with thermal solutions for CPO. Sivers contributes DFB lasers.
Sivers Photonics (CST Global) + imec joint technology: integrated assemblies of C-band (1530-1565nm) InP DFB lasers onto imec's silicon photonics platform. Began 2019.
DIC announced PPS film for mmWave at CES 2026 — adjacent to Sivers' mmWave wireless segment but no direct partnership disclosed.

named_customers.name: Unnamed automotive LiDAR customer
named_customers.scope: Strategic customer incorporating Sivers tech 'across all their platforms'; production ramp planned Q4 2026; revenue potential $53-138M over 8-10 year lifecycle (16-44% of 2025 sales)

named_customers.name: US Department of Defense (via NEMC)
named_customers.scope: $6.6M Year 2 funding via Microelectronics Commons program for US Defense Infrastructure modernization (May 19 2026)

Apple (via SiPH for consumer devices — referenced in primary-source Aleabit tweets but not officially confirmed by Sivers)

largest_known_shareholder.name: Erik Fällström / DDM Debt / Fällström Family Office
largest_known_shareholder.context: Co-founder Erik Fällström controls ~11.8% of votes via DDM Debt (where he is CEO) plus the Fällström Family Office. He is departing the board June 15 2026. His shareholding stays — but DDM has flagged intent to drive Sivers toward a 'broader investment company' which is in tension with the operational-pure-play thesis the US listing prep depends on.
